title: At the warung
goal: Order food and drink anywhere in Indonesia, from a plastic-stool warung to a restaurant — including the two questions you will be asked every single time: how spicy, and eat in or take away.
bekal: order a meal and a drink without pointing
say how spicy you want it, and mean it
ask for the bill, ask what a dish is, and say you liked it

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Warung nasi goreng
dialogs.intro: A busy street-side warung at eight in the evening. Mas Dedi runs the wok; Sarah has come alone.

lines.speaker: Dedi:
lines.id: Evening. What would you like to order?

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Nasi goreng satu, Mas. Pakai telur.
lines.id: One fried rice, please. With an egg.
lines.literal: rice fried one, Mr. use egg.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Es teh manis satu. Tidak pakai gula banyak, ya.
lines.id: One iced sweet tea. Not too much sugar, please.
lines.literal: ice tea sweet one. not use sugar many, yes.

lines.speaker: Dedi:
lines.text: Siap. Makan di sini atau bungkus?
lines.id: Right. Eat in or take away?
lines.literal: ready. eat at here or wrap?

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Makan di sini. Berapa lama, Mas?
lines.id: Eat in. How long will it take?
lines.literal: eat at here. how-much long, Mr?

lines.speaker: Dedi:
lines.id: Just five minutes. Please have a seat.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Terima kasih. Oh ya, ini apa, Mas?
lines.literal: thank you. oh yes, this what, Mr?

lines.speaker: Dedi:
lines.id: That's kerupuk. It's free, help yourself.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Wah, terima kasih! Nanti saya minta bon, ya.
lines.id: Thank you! I'll ask for the bill later.
lines.literal: wow, thank you! later I ask-for bill, yes.

notes: **Nasi goreng satu — the number goes last when ordering.** You will hear this everywhere: *kopi dua*, *es teh tiga*. It is not the neutral word order (*satu nasi goreng* is also fine) but it is what people say across a counter, because the dish is the important part.

**Pakai literally means "to use", and in a warung it means "with".** *Pakai telur* (with an egg), *pakai sambal* (with chilli sauce), *tidak pakai bawang* (no onion). If you have an allergy or a dietary restriction, *tidak pakai…* is the phrase that will keep you safe.

**Makan di sini atau bungkus?** *Bungkus* means "to wrap", and takeaway food in Indonesia is genuinely wrapped — often in paper and a plastic bag. Answering *bungkus* is all you need to say. 💬 You will also hear the English-derived *take away* and the Javanese-flavoured *dibungkus*.

**Sedikit pedas is not the same as mild.** Indonesian chilli tolerance is high, and *sedikit pedas* to a warung cook may still be considerable. If you truly cannot manage heat, say *tidak pedas sama sekali* ("not spicy at all") and expect to be asked again to be sure.

**Minta bon** is how you ask for the bill in a warung or simple restaurant; in smarter places you can say *minta bill* or *minta struk*. *Minta* means "to ask for" and it is one of the most useful verbs in the language.

grammars.title: Ordering: five sentence frames
body: Almost everything you will ever say in a restaurant fits one of these.

head: Frame
Example
English
rows: Do you have a vegetarian menu?

after: *Minta* is softer than *mau* and is the polite way to ask for something small — water, a spoon, the bill. *Mau* announces what you want; *minta* asks for it.
Adding *ya* to the end of any of these softens it further: *Tidak pakai sambal, ya.* Indonesians do this constantly, and it is the easiest way to sound polite rather than abrupt.

grammars.title: Food and drink you will meet in week one
body: Learn the building blocks and you can read most menus in the country.
after: Put two together and you have a dish: *nasi goreng* (fried rice), *mie goreng* (fried noodles), *ayam bakar* (grilled chicken), *ikan goreng* (fried fish), *sayur asem* (sour vegetable soup). The cooking method follows the ingredient — the same noun-then-description order you learned in Unit 7.

⚠️ *Babi* is pork. In a country with a large Muslim majority, most warung do not serve it, and asking loudly for it can be awkward. Look for the word *halal* or, in Bali and Chinese-Indonesian areas, for *babi* on the menu.

sections.title: Saying what you can and cannot eat

blocks.text: Indonesians take dietary restrictions seriously and will ask follow-up questions, so it pays to be able to say this clearly and calmly.

head: Indonesian
English
rows: Does this have meat in it?

blocks.text: ⚠️ Two hidden ingredients catch vegetarians out constantly: *terasi* (shrimp paste, in most sambal) and *kaldu ayam* (chicken stock, in most soup). The question to ask is *Pakai terasi?* — and asking it will earn you a nod of respect for knowing.

head: Indonesian
English
When
rows: Do I pay at the till?

blocks.text: Tipping is not expected in warung and street food. In restaurants the bill often already includes a service charge and *pajak* (tax) — look for *++* after the prices on the menu, which means both are added on top.

And one piece of etiquette that costs nothing: if you are eating and someone walks past, offer them food with *Mari, makan!* They will decline. Both halves of this exchange are ritual, and skipping your half is what gets noticed.

items: Tidak ____ sambal, saya tidak suka pedas.
